[] produced a powder with 99% protein content and reported turbidity reduction rates of ~95% using only 0.7 mg/L coagulant. As seen with defatted extracts, purified protein was “more effective for the treatment of low turbidity water” because it introduced lower concentrations of organic residues. Hounsinou et al. [] also stated “water treatment with this coagulant is inexpensive”, although the eight-step methodology for processing MO seeds—which includes of soxhlet extraction, microfiltration and lyophilisation—does not corroborate. For comparison, Jung et al. [] performed a five-step aqueous extraction that also reduced turbidity by 95%.

In further reading, tertiary processing did little to improve CFS capacity over secondary-processed extracts. Eman et al. [] concluded “that to include ultrafiltration step in the production process was considered as a loss, besides the waste of time and labour”. Ghebremichael et al. [] likewise found no improvement in turbidity reduction using purified extracts, though by measuring COD change they also found negligible organic residues in treated water.

An additional purpose of tertiary processing is to improve the interlaboratory robustness of MOCP testing. As the purity of an extract increases, the accuracy of MOCP concentration measurements also increase. This allows researchers to overcome differences in phytochemical profiles between MO cultivars and between seeds harvested under different conditions. It also allows researchers to isolate individual MOCPs to better study their properties. The benefits of tertiary processing are therefore limited to removing residual organic matter and enabling consistent MOCP research. For field applications, methods of protein purification are rarely employed.

3.5. Effects of MO seed coagulant dosing concentrations

MO seed coagulants were dosed at 2.5 – 350 mg/L in 16 of 25 reports [,,,,,,,–,]. Active MOCP concentrations vary between preparation methods, so correlations between pre-treatment turbidity, coagulant dose and turbidity reduction rate could not be established. For example, Delelegn et al. [] achieved 83.8% turbidity reduction in 208 NTU water using MO seed powder at 16 mg/L, and Chales et al. [] achieved 89.5% turbidity reduction in 200 NTU water using a defatted saline extract at 5 mg/L. However, Petersen et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction of 91.7% in 150 – 175 NTU water using a whole-seed aqueous extract at 200 mg/L. In these examples, pre-treatment turbidity readings and turbidity reduction rates were comparable, whereas optimal dosing concentrations varied significantly depending on the coagulant preparation methods and resultant concentrations of available MOCPs. As such, researchers should aim to trial MO seed coagulants at dynamic concentrations instead of relying on static doses from pre-existing publications. Even when processing methods are carried out identically, varying phytochemical profiles can affect MOCP concentration in unpredictable ways.

In 5 of 25 reports, MO seed coagulants were tested at concentrations higher than the common range of 2.5 – 350 mg/L. Jung et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 95% in 325 NTU wastewater using whole-seed aqueous extracts at 500 mg/L, and Addich et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 87.5% in 200 NTU wastewater using MO seed powder at 600 mg/L. Using computational modelling, Adesina et al. [] predicted a turbidity reduction of 99.3% in “> 800 NTU” water using a whole-seed aqueous extract at 3,000 mg/L; the accuracy of this model was reportedly verified via jar testing. Ng & Elshikh [] reported turbidity reduction rates of 94.9% using a defatted saline extract at 20,000 mg/L; pre-treatment turbidity was not reported, so it was unclear why elevated dosing concentrations were chosen in this instance. Due to the high risk of bias associated with Addich et al. [] and Adesina et al.’s [] reports, the utility of elevated coagulant dosing cannot be reliably assessed.

In one report, dosing concentration was unclear due to imprecise language such as “small quantity of clean water” and “two drops [of coagulant]” []. In a second report, dosing concentration was unclear because jar test volume was not reported and coagulant dose was consistently reported in “mg” and not “mg/L” []. Both reports received “lowest quality” judgements as they were not replicable. To enable replicability, precise measurements are necessary and encouraged.

Data pertaining to MO seed coagulant dosing ranges, optimal doses and treatment efficacy are displayed in Table 15. To investigate potential correlations between these variables, data from Table 15 was plotted onto three scatter graphs. No significant correlations were observed between pre-treatment turbidity and optimal coagulant dose (Fig 5), pre-treatment turbidity and optimal turbidity reduction rate (Fig 6) or optimal coagulant dose and optimal turbidity reduction rate (Fig 7). Pre-treatment turbidity values were unclear in several reports, so it was not possible to include every data set from Table 15 in these graphs. Therefore, the Figs 5–7 should be considered exploratory and not definitive.

Data from Table 15 is also plotted alongside judgements for overall research quality and overall risk of bias in Figs 8–9 and Fig 10. Each graph includes two trendlines: the first trendline includes data from all reports that were able to be included in the graph; the second excludes reports that received “high risk of bias” judgements. A comparison of these trendlines reveals an underestimation of treatment efficacy in all graphs when “high risk of bias” reports are considered. These findings suggest bias was not introduced intentionally to cause an overestimation of treatment efficacy. Figs 8–10 also show that “lower quality” or “lowest quality” research often resulted in below-average treatment efficacy, regardless of bias risk. This finding suggests jar testing with MO seed coagulants is a relatively technical undertaking that could benefit from standardised procedures.

3.6. Effects of chemical coagulant dosing concentrations

Arguments for the adoption of natural coagulants are largely responses to the shortcomings of chemical coagulants, with particular emphasis on alum. As such, alum was selected as a positive control in 8 of 25 reports. With appropriate dosing, alum is an effective and consistent coagulant: Amante et al. [] achieved 97.9% turbidity reduction in 53 NTU synthetic water using alum at 100 mg/L; Chales et al. [] achieved 98.0% turbidity reduction in 200 NTU well water using alum at 20 mg/L; Delelegn et al. [] achieved 98.4 – 99.1% turbidity reduction in 129 NTU and 208 NTU river waters using alum at 16 mg/L; Hounsinou et al. [] achieved ~95% turbidity reduction in 40 NTU lake water using alum at 40 mg/L, and; Shah et al. [,] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 98.4 – 99.2% in 82 NTU synthetic water using alum at 30 – 250 mg/L.

Conversely, inappropriate dosing can result in the misleading notion that alum is an ineffective coagulant. By extrapolation, this can lead to an overestimation of MO seed coagulant utility. Taiwo et al. [] demonstrated 19.1% turbidity reduction in 41 NTU reservoir water using alum at 5% w/v (50,000 mg/L) and Freitas et al. [] demonstrated 56.5% turbidity reduction in 38 NTU river water using alum at 2% w/v (20,000 mg/L). Both reports received “high risk of bias” judgements for this reason. As a guideline, appropriate dosing ranges for alum and MO seed coagulants were broadly comparable at 5 – 250 mg/L and 2.5 – 350 mg/L, respectively.

Hendrawati et al. [] were the only researchers to use an alternative to alum, employing polyaluminum chloride (PAC) as a positive control. At 100 mg/L, PAC and MO seed powder achieved respective turbidity reduction rates of 89.4 – 89.6% and 97.4 – 98.6% in both wastewater (320 – 350 NTU) and groundwater (220 – 230 NTU). In this instance, the natural coagulant outperformed the chemical coagulant at an identical dose. For tabulated data on chemical coagulant dosing, see Table 16.

In total, 16 of 25 reports did not include a chemical coagulant to compare the efficacy of MO seed coagulants with [,,,,,,–,–,,,]. Data may not have been generated, or it may have been omitted to avoid unfavourable comparisons between natural and chemical coagulants. Missing positive control data was a common cause of quality loss when assessing research quality. In future publications, reporting of full control data is encouraged.

3.7. Prevalence and outcomes of microbiological testing

Coliforms are Gram-negative bacteria prevalent in the gastrointestinal tracts and faeces of warm-blooded animals. As such, they can be indicators of faecal contamination and disease risk when detected in the environment. Coliforms of the genera Enterobacter, Klebsiella and Citrobacter can also be found in absence of faecal contamination, leading to the narrower classification of “faecal coliforms”: Gram-negative, thermotolerant bacteria that originate exclusively from the gastrointestinal tracts of warm-blooded animals. As a result of this reclassification, coliform bacteria are often referred to as “total coliforms” (TCF) and faecal coliform bacteria are often referred to as “thermotolerant coliforms” (TTC). Of particular interest to public health is the TTC E. coli and a shiga-like toxin-producing serotype of the species, E. coli 0157-H7. It is impractical to detect every pathogen in an environmental sample, so TCF, TTC and E. coli counts are routinely used to assess microbiological water quality and disease risk [].

Bacteriological jar testing was performed in 8 of 25 reports: four reports tested TCF native to their test waters [,,,]; four reports tested laboratory-grown E. coli at concentrations ranging from ~3 x 103 CFU/100ml to 1 x 108 CFU/100ml [,,,]. While these concentrations differ by many orders of magnitude, coliform concentrations can be as low as 0 CFU/100ml in well-managed wells and as high as 109 CFU/100ml in untreated wastewaters [,]. When using laboratory-grown organisms, researchers can simulate different water types by inoculating at appropriate microorganism concentrations.

Two publications found correlations between turbidity reduction and reduction in bacterial concentration: Jung et al. [] reported E. coli and turbidity reductions of ~95% when using an aqueous extract at 250 mg/L, and Delelegn et al. [] reported respective TCF and turbidity reductions of 62.5 – 97.5% and 73.1 – 87.0% when using MO seed powder at 16 – 80 mg/L. This correlation is important to prove because turbidity reduction without microbial load reduction can lead to a false sense of security in water treatment systems where bacteriological quality cannot be monitored.

Conversely, two publications did not find correlations between turbidity reduction and microbial load reduction. Using MO seed powder at 100 mg/L, Hendrawati et al. [] reported TCF reductions of 45% in groundwater and 80% in wastewater, whereas turbidity was reduced by 97.4% in groundwater and 98.6% in wastewater. Using an ammonium acetate buffer extract at 60 mg/L, Taiwo et al. [] reported TCF reductions of 58.2% and turbidity reductions of 40.8% in reservoir water.

Using a tertiary extract (99% protein), Hounsinou et al. [] reported 100% reduction in TCF and intestinal enterococci from respective pre-treatment concentrations of 5 x 104 CFU/100ml and 8.5 x 103 CFU/100ml. No methodological or results data is presented for their bacteriological testing, so this claim cannot be investigated further. Using an aqueous extract (particle size 250 – 400 μm, dose 300 mg/L), Shah et al. [] reported E. coli reductions of 99.9997%, from a pre-treatment concentration of 1 x 105 CFU/ml to a post-treatment concentration of < 1 CFU/ml. However, it is possible this methodology was flawed: E. coli were exposed to tap water for 3 h, which can lower microbial recovery rates via exposure to residual disinfectants. When exposed to free chlorine for 30 minutes, Wang et al. [] reported reductions in culturable E. coli of 99.98% (6.9 log to 3.1 log) at 0.2 mg/L chlorine and 99.9997% (log 6.9 to log 1.4) at 0.5 mg/L chlorine. Shah et al. [] conducted their experiments in the United Kingdom, where residual chlorine in tap water is maintained at ≤ 0.5 mg/L to sanitise distribution systems []. Additionally, no negative control data was reported (i.e., 0 mg/L coagulant) and the bacterial recovery method may be inadequate for jar testing: E. coli typically require 16 – 24 h of recovery on solid agar media when sampled from water, as opposed to 12 h []. In Shah et al.’s [] jar testing, alum (200 mg/L) also reduced E. coli concentration by 99.9997%. As such, their report received a “high risk of bias” judgement. It should be noted that the judgement was exclusive to the microbiological element of the report, and that the remainder of the report received a “highest quality” judgement.

Varkey [] tested a combined treatment of MO seed CFS and copper wire disinfection. Using ≥ 3 g/L copper for ≥ 3 h exposure, they reduced E. coli concentration to < 1 CFU/ml. Similarly, Keogh et al. [] tested a combined treatment of MO seed CFS and SODIS. Both the combined treatment and the negative control treatment (SODIS without CFS) reduced E. coli by 6 logs. However, in the negative control treatment E. coli concentration recovered by 5 logs in the 48 h post-treatment period, whereas in the combined treatment E. coli did not recover. Both reports received a “lowest quality” judgement, there were “some concerns” of bias in the former and a “high risk of bias” in the latter. Therefore, the utility of MO seed coagulants in combined treatments could not be reliably assessed.

Testing for faecal indicator organisms is a standard method of determining water quality. However, there is limited evidence to show that TCF, TTC and E. coli behave similarly to unrelated microorganisms, such as Gram-positive bacteria, protozoa, helminths and viruses, when exposed to CFS treatments. Electrostatic attraction and gravitational settling are physical phenomenon, and these organisms have great variations in scale and structure. As such, it is important to conduct MO seed CFS with specific pathogens where health and safety permits it. Petersen et al. [] trialled a whole-seed aqueous extract at 200 mg/L against Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts (~22 – 2,200 CFU/100ml) in wastewater. The treatment reduced oocyst concentration by 94 – 97.5%, irrespective of pre-treatment microbial load. In the same trial, turbidity was also reduced by 94.7%, demonstrating a correlation between turbidity reduction and microbial load reduction. When possible, testing with a wider variety of pathogens is recommended to show that microbial load reduction in MO seed CFS is not limited to coliform bacteria.

Outside of jar testing, two publications used the agar well diffusion method to assess the antimicrobial activity of MO seed extracts. Delelegn et al. [] trialled aqueous, acetone and methanol extracts at 50 mg/ml against three organisms: E. coli, Salmonella typhii and Shigella dysenteriae. All extracts formed zones of inhibition in all organisms, with the acetone and methanol extracts performing significantly better than the aqueous extract. Minimum inhibitory concentration was calculated to be 6.25 – 25.0 mg/ml. Taiwo et al. [] trialled an ammonium acetate buffer extract at 10 – 40 mg/ml against five isolates from local reservoir water: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Alcaligenes faecalis and three Klebsiella spp.. After 48 h of incubation, zones of inhibition formed in all isolates at 40 mg/ml and three of five isolates at 10 mg/ml, indicating a possible MIC. Considering the short duration of CFS (~1 – 3 h) and low coagulant doses (2.5 – 350 mg/L), it is unlikely that the antimicrobial activity of MO seeds contributes significantly to the disinfection of potable water. However, as discussed in Section 3.1.2, it is theorised that coagulant concentrations in MO seed sludges can be as high as 500 – 35,000 mg/L (0.5 – 35 mg/ml). Considering this, it is theorised that concentrated MO seed sludges possess antimicrobial activity, alongside potential larvicidal activity. This theory requires additional research, which could be used to demonstrate the safety of sludge use on arable farmland.

3.8. Effects of jar testing operational parameters

The most commonly recognised standard procedure for jar testing is “D2035: Standard Practice for Coagulation-Flocculation Jar Test of Water” by ASTM International []. The standard includes suggestions for key variables, interferences, apparatus and operational parameters. Regarding operational parameters, the standard suggests a three-stage model of CFS: “flash mix” (120 RPM, 1 min), “slow mix” (20 min) and “settling” (0 RPM). The standard also recommends withdrawing post-treatment water from “a point one half of the depth of the sample”, via pipet or siphon. There is no suggested revolution rate (RPM) for slow mixing; instead, the standard states “reduce the speed as necessary to the minimum required to keep floc particles uniformly suspended throughout the “slow mix” period”. Additionally, there is no suggested sedimentation time; the standard simply states “record the time required for the bulk of the [floc] particles to settle”. The operational parameters section concludes with the following statement: “The times given in [this section] are only suggestions”. Therefore, the only explicit operational parameters provided by the standard are the three-stage model of CFS, half-depth supernatant withdrawal and a revolution rate for flash mixing; all other parameters are subject researcher discretion [].

The apparatus section of the ASTM standard recommends using 1.5 L Griffin beakers with a multiple stirrer (a.k.a. jar tester/floc tester) of uniform paddle size and revolution rate; the minimum recommended volume is 1 L. The interferences section mentions three factors that can obfuscate treatment efficacy: Temperature change can cause convection currents that interfere with floc sedimentation; gas bubble formation can cause floc floatation that also interferes with sedimentation; biological activity between water sample and jar testing may alter coagulation characteristics. To account for potential interferences, the standard recommends two temperature measurements; one prior to coagulant dosing and one following 15 min of sedimentation. Visuals observations are recommended every 5 min during the “slow mix” period (i.e., flocculation); revolution rate, floc characteristics and presence/absence of gas bubbles can be recorded in these observations. Time elapsed between water sampling and jar testing should also “be kept to a minimum”, though no explicit time limit is suggested [].

In 14 of 25 reports, the standard three-stage model for CFS was used: a short period of fast stirring to facilitate particle collision for coagulation; a longer period of slow stirring to facilitate flocculation without breaking apart the flocs; and a long period with no stirring to facilitate sedimentation. Coagulation was conducted at 75 – 300 RPM for 20 s – 10 min (modal values: 100 RPM, 2 min). Flocculation was conducted at 10 – 60 RPM for 4 – 50 min (modal values: 20 RPM, 15 min). Sedimentation was typically allowed 30 – 120 min (modal values: 0 RPM, 60 min). Gaikwad & Munavalli [] adhered closely to standard operational procedures, with coagulation at 120 RPM for 1 min, tapered flocculation at 40 RPM for 10 min then 20 RPM for 10 min, and sedimentation at 0 RPM for 30 min; an optimal turbidity reduction rate of 88.6% was achieved using an aqueous extract of naturally-dried MO seeds. Three additional reports had loosely adherent operational parameters, with coagulation at 110 – 130 RPM for 1 – 2 min, flocculation at 25 – 36 RPM for 15 – 25 min, and sedimentation at 0 RPM for 30 – 240 min; these reports achieved optimal turbidity reduction rates of 89 – 95.9% using aqueous and saline extract of MO seed [,,]. In general, publications that adhered to the three-stage model of CFS achieved turbidity reduction rates of 80 – 96% with at least one type of MO seed coagulant [,,,,,–,–]. Adherence to the three-stage model appeared to be the determining factor for effective turbidity removal.

Ng & Elshikh [] conducted CFS with dynamic parameters to determine the effectiveness of various parameter combinations. Treated samples performed no better than untreated samples with coagulation parameters of 75 RPM for 7 min or with respective contact times of 10 s and 10 min during the coagulation and flocculation stages. Inadequate colloid–coagulant contact, due to low agitation speed and low coagulation duration, is believed to be the cause. In a study of varying sedimentation times (10 – 120 m), Camacho et al. [] found that turbidity reduction due to gravitational settling stopped at ≤ 60 min in untreated samples, whereas sedimentation in treated samples continued from 60 – 120 min, albeit slowly. Conversely, Addich et al. [] demonstrated comparable turbidity reduction rates following 60 min, 90 min and 120 min of sedimentation, suggesting no significant benefit to sedimentation times exceeding 60 min. While scarcely discussed in contemporary publications, microbial motility can enable cells to escape from flocs and sludges back into clarified supernatants []. As such, extended sedimentation times (> 60 m) are not recommended, particularly when microbial load is not being monitored.

Several research groups operated a two-stage model with either coagulation and sedimentation stages or flocculation and sedimentation stages. In four of these reports, a two-stage model was adequate and turbidity reduction rates were comparable to reports using the three-stage model [,,,]. Varkey [], who achieved turbidity reduction rates of 91.4 – 97.5%, conducted coagulation by “stirring vigorously” for 20 – 25 s and allowed 60 min for sedimentation. Following sedimentation, Varkey [] filtered the treated water through a fine-mesh cloth, so the efficacy of their method is incomparable to other reports. Additionally, three methodologies deviated from the three-stage model substantially and did not achieve effective CFS as a result. In the first example, samples were “agitated several times” and allowed to settle for 6 – 24 h. After settling, turbidity was reduced by ~38 – 50% in samples treated with MO seed aqueous extract and ~25 – 55% in untreated control samples []: this overlap resulted in a “high risk of bias” judgement. In a second example, dosed samples were “mixed for 3 min” and allowed to settle for 1 h, resulting in a maximum turbidity reduction of 40.77% []. In a third example, samples were vortexed for 10 s every 5 min for 2 h with no clear sedimentation period. Prior to a final filtration stage, MO seed powder reduced turbidity by 47.56% in treated samples []. These methodologies were neither replicable nor transparent due to imprecise language. Consequently, they received “lower quality” or “lowest quality” judgements and additional bias concern.

Data pertaining to jar test parameters and treatment efficacy are displayed in Table 17. To visualise this information, data from Table 17 were plotted onto a scatter graph (Fig 11). Treatments with atypical jar test parameters are shown to have limited turbidity reduction rates; treatments using atypical methods of coagulant processing (i.e., low MOCP concentration) are also shown to limit treatment efficacy. While there is no clear relationship between MO seed coagulant type and turbidity reduction rate, several of the included studies report superior properties in saline extracts over aqueous extracts [,,]. There are more than twenty-five coagulants included in Fig 11 because some researchers tested multiple coagulant types. Data collected from Hendrawati et al.’s [] report could not be included due to insufficient methodological detail. As with Figs 5–7, this graph should be considered exploratory and not definitive.

Data from Table 17 is also plotted alongside judgements for overall research quality and overall risk of bias in Fig 12. Reports with “low risk of bias” judgements exclusively conducted jar testing using a three-stage model of CFS. With the exception of Petersen et al. [], “highest quality” and “higher quality” reports also used a three-stage model of CFS. Lower treatment efficacy was predominantly observed in “lower quality” and “lowest quality” reports, as previously shown in Figs 8–10. These findings suggest the three-stage model of CFS is a reliable research method.

When conducting microbiological testing with laboratory-grown organisms, a preliminary naturalisation stage can also be considered. This is to facilitate interactions between microorganisms and clay-sized particles, which are ubiquitous in nature [,]. Implementing this stage can increase standardisation between research on natural water microbiomes and research on lab-grown microorganisms. In absence of relevant methodologies, the following parameters are suggested: agitation at 20 RPM for 15 min between microorganism inoculation and coagulant dosing.

A final consideration for jar testing parameters is the depth at which post-treatment water is sampled. At 33 – 42% oil content, MO seeds are rich in long-chain and very-long-chain fatty acids, which are less dense than water [,]. As a result, residual fatty acids will float to the water’s surface and form scum during sedimentation. Sampling this scum can return misrepresentative turbidity and microbiological readings, so it should be avoided. Scum formation is less of an issue in defatted MO seed extracts and tertiary-processed MOCPs. Five publications reported water sampling depth: Rasheed et al. [] sampled from a depth of 20 cm, Baptista et al. [] from a depth of 10 cm, Singh & Choubey [] from a depth of 5 cm, Jung et al. [] from mid-depth and Gaikwad & Munavalli [] from a depth of 1 cm. The ASTM standard suggests mid-depth water sampling, so Jung et al. [] were adherent in this respect []. It should also be noted that jar test volume ranged from 250 ml to 1 L in the included reports. Therefore, is it preferable to report water sampling depth as a fraction of vessel depth (e.g., “half-depth”), as opposed to reporting depth in centimetres, which is relative to vessel height.

To summarise, jar testing operational parameters were commonly designed from optimisation testing within the report, pre-existing scientific literature (their own research, or that of other researchers) or from unpublished optimisation testing conducted prior to published research. Standard procedures were not commonly referenced, and this was possibly a result of the ambiguous parameters suggested by the ASTM standard []. Moreover, it is likely each coagulant, or at least each group of related coagulants, has unique optimal parameters that cannot be listed in a standard procedure and can only be determined via optimisation testing. However, researchers should still strive to conduct temperature measurements and visual checks for gas bubble formation to account for sedimentation interference; these are valuable recommendations that can improve research quality [].

3.9. Physiochemical analyses

3.9.1. Effects of water treatment on pH.
MO seed coagulants are widely considered pH neutral, whereas chemical coagulants are known to acidify water and necessitate pH adjustment with industrial chemicals. As such, pre-and-post-treatment pH measurements were made in 12 of 25 reports to verify this point. Treatment with MO seed coagulants caused no significant pH changes in seven reports, in which pre-treatment pH ranged from 6.95 – 8.50 [,,,,,,]. MO seed coagulants caused minor pH decreases (<-0.35) in three reports, in which pre-treatment pH ranged from 6.60 – 7.39 [,,]: In Varkey’s [] report, disinfection with copper wire may also have altered pH. Hendrawati et al. [] reported significant increases in pH (+ 0.42 – 1.10) in all samples treated with MO seed powder at 80 – 100 mg/L. In textile mill wastewater (pH 5.10; turbidity 310 – 350 NTU), it is possible the neutralisation and sedimentation of acidic substances was responsible for these pH increases; in groundwater (pH 6.96; turbidity 205 – 230 NTU), pH increases were less easily explained. In a computational modelling publication, treatment with whole-seed aqueous extracts at 20,000 – 40,000 mg/L significantly decreased pH (-0.43 to -1.77) in 28 of 29 simulations. Pre-treatment pH was 7.97 in this instance, but pH change was not discussed by the researchers []. The WHO does not propose health-based guidelines for drinking water pH, but a range of 6.5 – 8.5 is suggested to prevent corrosion of distribution systems and preserve acceptability (i.e., taste, odour, appearance) []. In most instances, MO seed coagulants did not significantly affect water pH. Therefore, if pre-treatment readings are within the WHO-suggested range, satisfactory post-treatment readings can be expected.

To draw comparisons between MO seed coagulants and chemical coagulants, 6 of 25 reports monitored pH change in alum-treated waters and one in PAC-treated waters. Significant dose-dependent pH decreases were observed in three reports using alum [,,]. Amante et al. [] reported a pH decrease of 0.7 (pH 7.4 to pH 6.7) in waters treated with alum at 100 mg/L, although at pH 6.7, post-treatment readings still adhered to the WHO-suggested range (pH 6.5 – 8.5) []. Shah et al. [] stated “the pH of water treated with alum was slightly reduced” but no data was provided. Freitas et al. [] reported only minor pH changes of -0.10 – 0.18 in river water (pH 7.39) treated with alum at 2% w/v (20,000 mg/L); this finding is not fully understood.

Hendrawati et al. []—the only researchers to test an alternate chemical coagulant—reported pH decreases of -0.27 (pH 5.10 to pH 4.83) in PAC-treated wastewater and -1.75 (pH 6.96 to pH 5.21) in PAC-treated groundwater; PAC concentration was 100 mg/L in both instances.

A consideration for pH monitoring is the effect of acidification on microbiological testing. E. coli can tolerate a pH of 2.5 or less, and coliforms are defined by their ability to ferment lactose into acids and gas, so they are relatively acid resistant [,]. This may not be true of other test organisms, so pH changes should be considered when assessing microbial load reduction in waters treated with pH-altering coagulants, such as alum and PAC.

3.9.2. Effects of water treatment on DOC, COD, BOD and TDS.
Discussed in Section 3.1.2 are the disadvantages of natural coagulants caused by dissolved organic residues. Briefly, these residues can lower the acceptability of drinking water, increase post-treatment turbidity, worsen drinking water shelf-life and interact with chemical disinfectants to form harmful DBPs. Using a carbon analyser, DOC concentrations can be measured outright. Alternatively, COD can be measured to infer the concentration of chemically oxidisable residues, BOD can infer the concentration of residues oxidisable by microorganisms or TDS can infer the combined content of all dissolved organic and inorganic residues. Contemporary research is trending towards the use of MO seed extracts over MO seed powders, as they are believed to introduce lower concentrations of dissolved organic residues into treated waters.

Among the included reports, DOC, COD, BOD and TDS data inspired mixed discussion. Five reports that used authentic test water (i.e., water sampled from the field with no turbidity adjustment) observed significant reductions in dissolved residues: Taiwo et al. [] achieved respective COD and BOD reductions of 78.6% and 74.6% in reservoir water using an ammonium acetate buffer extract; Addich et al. [] achieved COD reductions of 58.8% in wastewater using MO seed powder; Hendrawati et al. [] observed reductions in COD and BOD in wastewater and groundwater using MO seed powder; Irikannu et al. [] reported respective TDS reductions of 57.8 – 83.3% and 54.5 – 83.6% in borehole water and sachet water using an aqueous extract of MO seed, and; Kenea et al. [] reported respective COD and TDS reductions of 3.57 – 71.93% and 72.81 – 92.12% in river water using a blend of MO seed and Aloe vera (1:1). Additionally, Baptista et al. [] reported decreased DOC using saline extracts of MO seed, whereas aqueous extracts increased DOC; authentic test water was also used in this instance.

Conversely, three reports that used synthetic or turbidity-adjusted test water observed increases in DOC. Chales et al. [] reported increased DOC in kaolin-adjusted well water treated with MO seed powders, aqueous extracts, saline extracts and defatted versions of each of the previous. When dosed optimally (20 mg/L), there were insignificant differences between the rates of DOC increase among the six coagulants; at 200 mg/L, there were larger DOC increases with aqueous and saline extracts than with MO seed powders. Jung et al. [] reported increased DOC in kaolin-adjusted wastewater treated with aqueous extracts of MO seed. Camacho et al. [] reported increased DOC in synthetic water treated with MO seed powder, defatted MO seed powder and ethanol-saline extracts of MO seed.

From these findings, the following theory is proposed: authentic test waters typically have high native organic load. When treating authentic waters, the increase in organic residues inherent to natural coagulants can be offset by effective reduction of the native organic load. Conversely, synthetic and kaolin-adjusted waters have low native organic load. When treating these water types, the increase in organic residues from natural coagulants cannot be offset because the native organic load is lower that what is introduced by coagulant dosing. Therefore, it is suggested that DOC, COD, BOD and TDS experiments are best performed with authentic test waters and avoided when using synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters, particularly when inorganic clouding agents, such as kaolin, are used.

Five reports that tested with authentic water received “lower quality” or “lowest quality” judgements and were associated with high bias risk or bias concerns [,,,,]. Conversely, the reports that tested with synthetic water received “highest quality” or “higher quality” judgements and “low risk of bias” judgements [,,]. Due to this imbalance, additional research is required to validate or refute the theory.

3.9.3. Effects of water treatment on sludge properties.
Despite the commonly discussed benefits of MO seed sludge over chemical sludges, none of the included publications reported sludge volumes or sludge properties for waters treated with MO seed coagulants or alum. Additionally, visual observations on sludge and floc properties were rare. Such measurements and observations are relatively simple to make, so they should be considered in future research.

3.10. Methods of data analysis

Methods of statistical analysis were disclosed in 20 of 25 reports. Twelve used mean values ± standard deviation, analysis of variance (ANOVA) and/or Tukey’s test at 95% confidence [–,,,,,,,]. Three research groups used response surface methodology [,,]. Petersen et al. [] used a normal linear regression model, validated by quantile–quantile plots and a residual plot; the model was reduced by backward stepwise regression at 95% confidence. Five reports did not disclose analytical methods [,,,,]. Missing methodological data was commonly associated with “lower quality” and “lowest quality” judgements and increased risk of bias.

4. Summary of findings

- The systematic review was completed to PRISMA 2020 standards using Cochrane tools modified for in vitro laboratory studies. The reliability of contemporary research was assessed and many recommendations were made to guide future research towards high-quality, unbiased testing and emerging theories; the aims of the review were therefore completed.

- The scope of the systematic review was limited due to its small research team and budget. Screening was limited to the first ten results for each search term (n = 21) within each search year (2014 – 2024) in each academic database and search engine used (n = 3); toll access reports were also excluded from data collection. Nonetheless, 25 jar testing reports were included, from which 511 data points were collected and synthesised.

- The reliability of contemporary jar testing with MO seed coagulants was inconsistent. Research quality assessments returned nine “highest quality” or “higher quality” judgments and 16 “lower quality” or “lowest quality” judgements. Risk of bias assessments returned seven “low risk of bias” judgements, 12 “some concerns” judgements, and six “high risk of bias” judgements. Reports with “high risk of bias” judgements were found to underestimate the efficacy of CFS with MO seed coagulants.

- The most concerning findings were inadequate reporting of negative control data in 8 of 25 reports, absent positive control data in 16 of 25 reports, inappropriate positive control dosing concentrations in two reports, and failure to declare the age of MO seeds (a confounding factor) in 23 of 25 reports.

- MO seeds retained high CFS capacity when they were dried prior to storage and stored in air-tight containers to prevent the reuptake of moisture. Drying temperatures exceeding 90°C (363.2 K) damaged CFS capacity.

- Methods of coagulant processing can be categorised as primary (MO seed powders), secondary (MO seed extracts) and tertiary (purified MOCPs). Powders were studied in 9 of 25 reports, extracts were studied 18 of 25 and purified protein was studied in one report. Extracts were typically aqueous (n = 15) or saline (n = 6).

- Saline extracts commonly outperformed aqueous extracts, and aqueous extracts rarely outperformed MO seed powders when tested in parallel. This is theoretically a result of MOCP self-association in aqueous extracts and modulation of protein–protein interactions in saline extracts; this theory requires additional research.

- Due to their comparable molecular masses, occurrence as oligomers, tendency to self-associate, thermostability, and affinity for carbohydrate and chitin binding, MOCPs are believed to be lectins with hevein-like binding domains.

- MO seed coagulants were commonly tested at 2.5 – 350 mg/L. Overdose can result in the suspension of excess coagulant and possible resuspension of colloids and pathogens. There was no consensus optimum dose because MOCP concentrations vary between seed batches and methods of processing.

- CFS with MO seed coagulants consistently achieved turbidity reduction rates of 80 – 96% when the three-stage model of CFS was adhered to. Deviation from the three-stage model was the predominant cause of ineffective CFS. Modal operating parameters were: coagulation at 100 RPM for 2 min, flocculation 20 RPM for 15 min, and sedimentation at 0 RPM for 60 min.

- CFS with alum achieved turbidity reduction rates of 95.0 – 99.2% when dosed optimally (16 – 250 mg/L). As such, alum commonly outperformed MO seed coagulants.

- CFS with alum was reported to acidify water, whereas CFS with MO seed coagulants was reportedly pH neutral. These reports were verified by contemporary publications.

- CFS with alum was also reported to produce high volumes of toxic sludge, whereas CFS with MO seed coagulants was reported to produce low volumes of biodegradable sludge. Sludges are not being studied in contemporary publications, so these reports could not be verified or refuted.

- When DOC, BOD and COD experiments were performed with authentic test waters, MO seed coagulants reduced oxidisable residue concentrations significantly. When synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters were used, MO seed coagulants increased oxidisable residue concentrations.

- Microbiological testing was uncommon and focussed primarily on coliforms and E. coli. Correlations between microbial load reduction and turbidity reduction were found in three reports, whereas two reports demonstrated no significant correlation. Microbiological methodologies were occasionally flawed.

4.1. Recommendations

- Future research can benefit from improved standardisation and data reporting practices. To test the theory that MO seed coagulants are viable alternatives to chemical coagulants, both natural and chemical coagulants must be tested in parallel. To demonstrate CFS is more effective than gravitational settling, tests must contain untreated negative control samples (i.e., 0 mg/L coagulant). Full data must be reported for both positive and negative controls.

- Standardisation can also be improved by reporting MO seed age and storage conditions, adhering to the three-stage model of CFS and adhering to the common coagulant dosing range. Standardisation assists the research community in identifying causes of favourable and unfavourable results by reducing the range of independent variables and impact of confounding factors.

- Primary-processed coagulants are practical for use in rural sub-Saharan Africa, the region most affected by economic water scarcity and energy poverty. Whole-seed MO powder should not be neglected in favour of secondary-processed extracts and defatting, which can be impractical and economically unviable when prepared using complexed methods and electrical equipment. When testing extracts, consider testing MO seed powder in parallel as a control measure; extracts do not always outperform dry powder.

- Sludge disposal is a major expense of CFS, so sludge research requires more attention than it is currently receiving. Measuring and comparing sludge volumes in waters treated with MO seed coagulants and chemical coagulants is a simple way to contribute to sludge research.

- DOC, BOD, COD and TDS experiments are best performed with authentic test waters. Synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters can have atypically low pre-treatment organic load, particularly when inorganic clouding agents, such as kaolin, are used. Measuring dissolved residues in non-authentic waters may return misleading results.

- Researchers with adequate facilities should strive to include microbiological measurements in their jar testing experiments to expand the currently-limited evidence base. Where health and safety permits it, alternate waterborne pathogens should also be trialled to ensure effective microbial load reduction with non-coliform organisms. Synthetic water (i.e., tap water, distilled water) is not suitable for microbiological testing.

If researchers wish to participate in standardised jar testing with MO seed coagulants, consider the reporting criteria and suggestions listed in Table 18. The reporting criteria in Table 18 may also benefit researchers working on alternate natural coagulants.

title: Association of erythropoietin gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C>T/G) with diabetic retinopathy in Type 2 diabetes mellitus patients of Punjabi population in Pakistan
content:
Abstract
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and is influenced by genetic factors. We investigated the association between the erythropoietin (EPO) gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) and DR risk in a Punjabi Pakistani cohort of adults with T2DM. In a case–control design, 573 T2DM patients (294 with DR, 279 controls without retinopathy, CDR) were genotyped by ARMS-PCR. The protective CC genotype was significantly more frequent in controls (96.77%) than in cases (30.61%) and was associated with markedly reduced DR risk (OR = 68; 95% CI 33.468–138.162; p < 0.001). Conversely, the GG and TT genotypes were absent in controls but present in DR patients (27.55% and 21.43%, respectively) and were strongly associated with increased DR risk (p < 0.001). Allele-level analysis mirrored genotype findings: the C allele predominated in controls (98.39%) but was significantly less frequent in cases (39%), while G and T alleles were enriched among DR patients (p < 0.001). Together, genotype- and allele-based results indicate that the rs1617640 C variant is protective against DR in this Punjabi T2DM population, whereas G and T variants increase DR susceptibility.

Introduction
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most severe microvascular complications associated with diabetes mellitus, and it is a leading cause of blindness worldwide, particularly among working-age adults [–]. The global burden of DR is escalating alongside the increasing prevalence of T2DM, particularly in low- and middle-income countries like Pakistan. In 2020, the global prevalence of DR was estimated at 103 million, with projections indicating a rise to 161 million by 2045 []. This alarming trend is largely driven by the rapidly growing diabetic population [], especially in regions such as Africa, the Middle East, North Africa, and the Western Pacific. The prevalence of DR is notably high in Africa (35.90%), North America and the Caribbean (33.30%), and the Middle East and North Africa (32.90%), with significant rates also reported in the Western Pacific (19.20%), Europe (18.75%), South East Asia (16.99%), and South and Central America (13.37%) []. Among Asian patients with T2DM, the prevalence of DR is estimated to be around 28% [–]. Despite advances in T2DM management, the incidence of DR continues to rise, emphasizing the urgent need for a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to its development and progression. The pathogenesis of DR is multifactorial, involving chronic hyperglycemia, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and genetic predisposition []. While the roles of glycemic control and systemic factors are well-documented, the genetic component of DR is less understood. Recent studies have increasingly focused on identifying genetic markers that may contribute to the susceptibility to DR, with the aim of developing targeted prevention and treatment strategies [–].

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone that plays a critical role in stimulating erythropoiesis, the process of producing red blood cells, particularly under hypoxic conditions []. The activation of the EPO gene occurs when hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF-1) bind to its promoter region, leading to increased EPO production []. Beyond its primary role in erythropoiesis, EPO has been recognized as a potent angiogenic factor, contributing to the formation of new blood vessels [,]. This dual function of EPO in both erythropoiesis and angiogenesis implicates it in various physiological and pathological processes, including retinal health, where its angiogenic properties may influence conditions such as DR. The DR is characterized by damage to the retinal blood vessels, primarily due to chronic hyperglycemia-induced retinal hypoxia, which activates hypoxia-inducible factors that upregulate EPO and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [].

The rs1617640 polymorphism in the promoter region of the EPO gene has garnered significant attention due to its impact on EPO expression and its potential association with microvascular complications of DR. The T allele of rs1617640 has been linked to higher levels of EPO in the vitreous body [], suggesting its role in DR pathogenesis, particularly in promoting retinal neovascularization in proliferative diabetic retinopathy []. Although some studies have found significant associations between rs1617640 and DR [,,–], others have reported no significant link [–]. Specifically, the T allele was associated with the risk of DR in European-Americans [] and North Indians [] with T2DM. These mixed findings underscore the need for further research, particularly in diverse populations, to clarify the genetic factors contributing to DR.

In Pakistan, where the prevalence of T2DM is high [] and the population is genetically diverse [–], understanding the genetic risk factors for DR is of particular importance. The Punjabi population, in particular, represents a unique genetic pool with potential variations in DR susceptibility that have not been thoroughly investigated. This study was aimed to explore the association between the EPO gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) and the risk of developing DR in Punjabi patients with T2DM.

Methods

Participants

This case-control study included 573 Punjabi adults with T2DM recruited from hospitals in Sheikhupura and Lahore, Pakistan, between March 2023 and May 2024. The participants were categorized into two groups: the diabetic retinopathy (DR) group, consisting of 294 subjects with T2DM and retinopathy, and the control group (CDR), consisting of 279 subjects with T2DM but without retinopathy. The diagnosis of T2DM was based on clinical features and guidelines outlined by the Expert Committee Report of the American Diabetes Association. Retinopathy status was graded according to the criteria established by the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study [–]. Inclusion criteria for the DR group included individuals with retinopathy as the primary condition, diagnosed with diabetes at age 30 or older, and having an HbA1c level of 6.5% or higher. For the CDR group, participants were included if they had fasting plasma glucose levels of 150 mg/dL or higher, a duration of T2DM of at least five years, were diagnosed with diabetes at age 30 or older, and exhibited no microvascular or macrovascular complications. Individuals with type 1 diabetes or other ocular conditions such as optic neuropathy, dense cataract, or glaucoma were excluded from the study. HbA1c levels and blood urea nitrogen were measured from blood samples of all participants. Serum cholesterol, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels were assessed using standard kits (Cell Biolabs, Inc.). Additionally, body mass index (BMI) and blood pressure were recorded. The study protocol received approval from the Ethical review committee of Institute of Molecular Biology and Biotechnology, the University of Lahore (via letter No., Ref.IMBB/BBBC/22/230, dated December 15, 2022), and complied with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants of the study were properly informed about the purpose of the study and were asked to complete the designed questionnaire. A written informed consent was obtained, and the objective of the research study and method of blood sampling were explained to all the participating individuals in detail.

Inclusivity in global research

Additional information regarding the ethical, cultural, and scientific considerations specific to inclusivity in global research is included in the Supporting Information (S1 Checklist)

Sampling, DNA extraction, and genotyping

Peripheral venous blood (10 mL) was collected from each participant, and genomic DNA was extracted using the phenol-chloroform extraction method (S1 File). Genotyping of the polymorphisms was performed using a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) followed by DNA sequencing. The target gene was amplified using ARMS-PCR (Amplification-Refractory Mutation System-Polymerase Chain Reaction) for subsequent analysis. The specific target sequence was retrieved from the NCBI-dbSNP database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/snp/) using the SNP ID rs1617640. Tetra primers for ARMS-PCR were designed to amplify the target gene fragments (Fig 1). Primer design was carried out using SnapGene software (https://www.snapgene.com/), and the primers (Table 1) were synthesized by Macrogen, South Korea, at a scale of 50 nM. A stock solution at a concentration of 100 pmol/µL and a working solution of 10 pmol/µL were prepared and stored at −20°C.

For each PCR reaction, 1 µL of genomic DNA (50 ng) was used as the template in a 25 µL reaction mixture, which included 0.125 µL (0.63 units) of Taq polymerase, 2 µL of 2 mM dNTPs, 0.7 µL of each outer primer, 0.3 µL of each inner primer, 2 µL of MgCl₂, 2.5 µL of 10X Taq buffer, and 15.375 µL of distilled water. The PCR amplification protocol included an initial denaturation at 95°C for five minutes, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 30 seconds, annealing at 54°C for one minute, and extension at 72°C for 50 seconds. A final extension was performed at 72°C for ten minutes, followed by a holding step at 4°C. The PCR products were then analyzed on a 1% agarose/TAE gel under UV illumination to determine the ARMS-PCR banding patterns and genotypes. The observed band sizes were 169 bp for the mutant alleles and 475 bp for the wild-type allele corresponding to the rs1617640 C > T/G polymorphism. Allelic data were compiled in an MS Excel spreadsheet.

For further validation, the PCR products were sent to Celemics, Inc., South Korea, for commercial DNA sequencing using the BTSeq (Barcode-Tagged Sequencing) platform. The resulting sequences were analyzed for targeted peaks using SnapGene software. Multiple sequence alignments (MSA) were generated using CLUSTAL-W, as implemented in BioEdit software [], to visualize the rs1617640 C > T/G polymorphism in the aligned sequences.

Statistical analysis

Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 20 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The significance of allelic frequency differences was assessed using the Chi-square test, with p-values calculated to determine statistical significance. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed to evaluate the strength of the associations. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD).

Results

Demographic and clinical characteristics of the sampling

The demographic and clinical characteristics of the study subjects in both DR and CDR groups were analyzed and compared (Table 2). Among the participants, the DR group included 114 males and 180 females, while the control group comprised 149 males and 130 females. Key findings from this analysis revealed significant differences between the DR and CDR groups in terms of the duration of T2DM, HbA1c levels, fasting blood glucose (FBG), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and systolic blood pressure (SBP). Specifically, the DR group had a longer duration of T2DM (p < 0.001), higher HbA1c levels (p = 0.0054), and elevated SBP (p < 0.001) compared to the control group. In contrast, the control group exhibited significantly higher levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL (p < 0.001 for all), suggesting potential differences in lipid profiles between the groups. These clinical differences underscore the complex interplay of factors contributing to the development and progression of diabetic retinopathy. No significant difference was observed in diastolic blood pressure (DBP) between the two groups (p = 0.116), and the body mass index (BMI) was similar between both groups (p = 0.56), suggesting that these factors may not be as strongly associated with the presence of retinopathy in this cohort.

Differential distribution of genotypes and alleles between DR and CDR

To examine the distribution of genotypes and alleles between the DR and CDR groups, we first visualized the genotypic and allelic patterns. The results indicated that genotypes and alleles were not uniformly distributed between the case and control groups (Fig 2a-b). The normal CC genotype was predominantly found in the control group (Fig 2c) but was also present in the case group. In contrast, the case group showed a higher frequency of mutant genotypes, particularly the homozygous GG and TT combinations (Fig 2d-e), compared to the heterozygous CT and CG combinations (Fig 2f-g) or the double mutant TG combination (Fig 2h). A minor presence of the trisomy genotype CTG was also observed in the case group (Fig 2i). Regarding allelic distribution, the normal C allele was predominantly observed in the control group (Fig 2j) and was also present in the case group. The mutant alleles G and T were more abundant in the case group (Fig 2k-l). Notably, the distribution of the G allele was restricted to the case group, while the T allele was predominantly observed in the case group with a minor presence in the control group (Fig 2l). These findings suggest a differential distribution of genotypes and alleles between the case and control groups, with a pronounced presence of mutant genotypes and alleles in the case group. The observed differential distribution of genotypes and alleles led for the subsequent association analysis.

Association of rs1617640 C > T/G polymorphism with diabetic retinopathy

The analysis of genotype and allele frequencies for the EPO polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) between the CDR and DR groups reveals significant associations with the occurrence of diabetic retinopathy (Table 3). The genotype distribution shows a stark contrast between the two groups. In the CDR group, the CC genotype was overwhelmingly prevalent, observed in 96.77% of individuals, while it was significantly less frequent in the DR group, where only 30.61% of participants exhibited this genotype. This substantial difference is reflected in the odds ratio of 68, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 33.468–138.162, and a highly significant p-value of less than 0.001, indicating a strong protective effect of the CC genotype against the development of DR.

Conversely, the GG and TT genotypes, which were completely absent in the CDR group, were relatively common in the DR group, observed in 27.55% and 21.43% of individuals, respectively. The presence of these genotypes in the DR group is associated with significantly lower odds ratios (0.724 for GG and 0.786 for TT), both with p-values less than 0.001, suggesting a strong association between these genotypes and an increased risk of developing diabetic retinopathy. Additionally, the heterozygous CT genotype was more prevalent in the DR group (10.20%) compared to the CDR group (3.23%), with an odds ratio of 0.293 and a p-value of 0.001, further indicating its potential role in susceptibility to DR.

The allele frequency analysis further supports these findings. The C allele, which was nearly universal in the CDR group (98.39%), was significantly less frequent in the DR group (39%), corresponding to an odds ratio of 95.41 and a highly significant p-value of less than 0.001. In contrast, the G and T alleles, absent or rare in the CDR group (0% and 1.61%, respectively), were much more common in the DR group (32% for G and 29% for T). These alleles showed significantly lower odds ratios (0.68 for G and 0.04 for T) with p-values less than 0.001, indicating a strong association with diabetic retinopathy.

In sum, the data demonstrate a significant differential distribution of EPO polymorphism genotypes and alleles between the control and diabetic retinopathy groups. The CC genotype and C allele appear to be protective against diabetic retinopathy, while the GG, TT genotypes, and G and T alleles are strongly associated with an increased risk of developing this condition. These findings suggest that specific genetic variations in the EPO locus may play a critical role in the susceptibility to diabetic retinopathy.

Discussion
This study provides a detailed analysis of the association between EPO gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) and the risk of DR in a cohort of Punjabi patients with T2DM. The findings align with existing literature, highlighting the role of genetic variations in the EPO locus in influencing DR susceptibility, a major complication of diabetes [].

Our results demonstrate a pronounced difference in the distribution of genotypes and alleles between the DR and CDR groups. The protective role of the CC genotype, overwhelmingly prevalent in the control group, mirrors findings from studies such as one conducted on Australian descendants, which identified a significant association between the GG genotype and increased DR risk []. Similarly, there is evidence suggesting a 1.6-fold increased risk of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) in individuals with the GG genotype [], underscoring the susceptibility associated with this variant. However, our study differs in that the GG and TT genotypes were entirely absent in the control group, suggesting a stronger protective effect of the CC genotype in our Punjabi cohort, with an odds ratio of 68. Mechanistically, rs1617640 lies in the EPO promoter and has been shown to alter promoter activity and EPO expression in an allele-dependent manner [,]. Because erythropoietin is a potent retinal angiogenic and pro-survival factor implicated in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, a genotype/allele associated with lower EPO expression (the CC variant in our cohort) plausibly confers protection against pathological retinal neovascularization, whereas alleles that increase EPO expression promote DR — a point supported by existing genetic and meta-analytic studies [,].

The GG and TT genotypes, relatively common in the DR group, were associated with lower odds ratios (0.724 for GG and 0.786 for TT), indicating these genotypes may predispose individuals to DR. This observation aligns with previous research identifying the T allele of rs1617640 as a risk factor for PDR and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in European-Americans []. Notably, the rs1617640, rs507392, and rs551238 polymorphisms in the EPO gene were first investigated regarding their potential association with PDR and ESRD in European-Americans, where the T allele was shown to play a functional role in EPO expression []. Since the initial work [], the relationship between these genetic variants and DR has been evaluated in various populations, with mixed results. Some studies have reported positive associations with the G or T alleles, as seen in research on Australian descendants, Han Chinese, and North Indians [,,]. For instance, the T allele was associated with an increased risk of DR in North Indians with T2DM [], supporting the notion that this allele may be a risk factor in certain ethnic groups, as also suggested by our study where the C allele showed a protective effect. Conversely, other studies have found no significant association between these alleles and DR, as observed in research conducted on South Indians, Iranians, and Italians [–]. This disparity in findings across different populations suggests that the impact of these polymorphisms on DR risk may be influenced by ethnic and genetic backgrounds, environmental factors, or both.

Further supporting our findings, the heterozygous CT genotype also showed a higher prevalence in the DR group, with an odds ratio of 0.293, indicating its potential role in increasing susceptibility to DR. This is consistent with earlier studies that recognized higher DR risk in GG homozygotes in Han Chinese and North Indian populations [,]. However, the variability in results across studies, as noted in a meta-analysis, highlights the complexity of the genetic underpinnings of DR []. The meta-analysis, which included studies from diverse populations, revealed an association between the rs1617640 polymorphism and diabetic microvascular complications, but found no significant link between the polymorphism and DR risk in Asians or Australians.

The allele frequency analysis in our study revealed that the C allele was significantly more common in the control group, while the G and T alleles were more prevalent in the DR group. The nearly universal presence of the C allele in the control group (98.39%) and its much lower frequency in the DR group (39%) underscore its protective effect. This observation is consistent with the protective role of the C allele, as previously reported in European-Americans [], and contrasts with the T allele’s effect observed in other populations. The differential distribution of these genotypes and alleles suggests that the EPO gene polymorphism plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of DR. The protective effect of the CC genotype and C allele, coupled with the increased risk associated with the GG, TT genotypes, and G and T alleles, provides valuable insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying DR. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature emphasizing the importance of genetic screening in T2DM patients, particularly those with a family history of DR, to identify individuals who may benefit from more aggressive management of their glycemic control and other risk factors.

However, as with previous studies, our research is not without limitations. The case-control design, while effective for identifying associations, does not establish causality. Further longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the causal relationship between EPO polymorphism and DR development. Additionally, while our study focused on a Punjabi population, the findings may not be generalizable to other ethnic groups. Future research should explore the role of EPO polymorphisms in diverse populations to better understand the global relevance of these genetic markers. The observed differences in genotype distribution between the DR and CDR groups may also be influenced by demographic and clinical factors such as age, diabetes duration, glycemic control, and lipid profiles. For instance, the DR group had significantly higher HbA1c levels and longer diabetes duration, both of which are known to exacerbate retinal damage. Additionally, lipid profiles, including elevated cholesterol and triglyceride levels in the CDR group, may contribute to the development and progression of DR. In this study, the control group exhibited elevated levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL, which are commonly associated with cardiovascular diseases. Interestingly, these lipid abnormalities might also play a protective role by limiting the progression of DR. It is important to further explore how lipid metabolism interacts with genetic factors such as EPO polymorphisms to influence DR development. These heterogeneities should be considered when interpreting the findings, as they may affect the susceptibility to DR in different subgroups. The dual role of erythropoietin in retinal health presents a paradox. While its angiogenic properties may promote retinal blood vessel repair, in severe diabetic retinopathy, these effects may exacerbate pathological neovascularization. This highlights the complex nature of EPO’s influence on the retina, particularly in patients with advanced diabetes, where excessive angiogenesis may lead to proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

In conclusion, this study provides compelling evidence that the EPO gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) is significantly associated with the risk of diabetic retinopathy in Punjabi patients with T2DM. The protective effect of the CC genotype and C allele, along with the increased risk conferred by the GG, TT genotypes, and G and T alleles, underscores the critical role of genetic factors in the pathogenesis of DR.

title: The Drosophila G protein-coupled receptor, GulpR, is essential for lipid mobilization in response to nutrient-limitation
content:
Abstract
Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) of the intestinal epithelium are major regulators of metabolism and energy homeostasis. This is mainly due to their expression and secretion of enteroendocrine peptides (EEPs). These peptides serve as hormones that control many aspects of metabolic homeostasis including feeding behavior, intestinal contractions, and utilization of energy stores. Regulation of EEP production and release depends largely on EEC-exclusive G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that sense nutrient levels. Here we report the characterization of a GPCR expressed principally in EECs, which we have named GulpR due to its role in the response to nutrient stress. We show that GulpR regulates transcription of the EEP Tachykinin (Tk) and that both GulpR and Tk are essential for the transcriptional response that promotes survival of nutrient limitation. Oral infection with V. cholerae also activates expression of GulpR, Tk, and lipid mobilization genes. However, Tk does not play a role in regulation of lipid mobilization genes during infection and does not impact survival. Our findings identify a role for GulpR and Tk in survival during starvation and suggest that, although starvation and infection result in significant mobilization of energy stores, the signal transduction systems that regulate the metabolic response to each are distinct.

Author summary

Humans and other animals, including Drosophila, catabolize dietary nutrients such as polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins into simple sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids, respectively, to generate the energy that fuels essential cellular processes like cell division, ion transport, muscle contraction, and more. The ability to adapt to changes in nutrient availability and energy demand is therefore crucial for homeostasis and survival. Nutrient scarcity and the energy demands of an immune response against pathogenic infection require utilization of the body’s own lipid and glycogen stores. This adaptive response largely relies on the ability of the intestine to sense and respond to a variety of stimuli, including microbes and dietary nutrients. Here, we have characterized a Drosophila melanogaster receptor that is expressed in a rare intestinal cell type with endocrine function. We report that this receptor regulates production of peptide hormones that are known to impact metabolic homeostasis and discover that one of these peptide hormones is crucial for utilization of systemic lipid stores under nutrient limitation but not infection stress. Our findings therefore indicate that lipid mobilization in response to nutrient limitation and infection are regulated via different mechanisms.

Introduction
Maintenance of metabolic homeostasis is crucial for the health span and life span of living organisms. This requires matching food consumption and catabolism to the energy expended. This balance is achieved in part through the action of gut-derived peptide hormones produced in enteroendocrine cells (EECs) []. EECs comprise the largest endocrine organ in the body, secreting more than 20 different enteroendocrine peptides (EEPs) [–]. EEPs can act in a paracrine fashion to regulate nutrient absorption, gut motility, epithelial renewal and other processes within the intestinal epithelium or in an endocrine fashion to regulate appetite, satiety, metabolism, and energy expenditure. Appropriate EEP expression and secretion relies on the ability of EECs to sense nutritional status and nutrient intake via systemic and intestinal signals, respectively. This is achieved, in large part, by the action of cell-autonomous G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are cell membrane-associated receptors that activate a signal transduction cascade in response to binding small molecules or peptides. In EECs, GPCRs respond to nutrients, metabolites secreted by the intestinal microbiota, bile acids, neuropeptides, or other molecules by regulating EEP expression and exocytosis-mediated secretion [,,].

Drosophila melanogaster has been used extensively as a model organism for the study of gastrointestinal (GI) processes as its intestine shares functional homology with the mammalian GI tract [,]. The adult Drosophila intestinal epithelium is subdivided into foregut, midgut, and hindgut sections []. The Drosophila midgut epithelium is composed of intestinal stem cells and two mature cell types: enterocytes (ECs), and enteroendocrine cells (EECs). While ECs are most abundant, EECs account for 5–10% of cells in the intestinal epithelium []. As in humans, Drosophila EEPs play crucial roles in regulating both intestinal physiology and systemic metabolism [–].

The Drosophila midgut can be subdivided into three regions (anterior, middle, posterior), exhibiting unique functional properties [,]. The microbiota of the fly resides mainly in the anterior midgut (AMG), which is also the compartment responsible for metabolism of complex macromolecules such as polysaccharides, fats, and proteins. Here we focus on regulation of the EEP Tachykinin (Tk), which is essential for innate immune signaling and lipid homeostasis in the AMG [,,]. Tk has also been shown to impact lipid reserves in the Drosophila fat body, which is the main site of energy storage in the fly and functionally analogous to human adipose tissue and the liver [,–].

To survive starvation or infection, animals must mobilize stores to meet their energy requirements [–]. Here we describe an orphan GPCR we have named GulpR that is specifically expressed in EECs, regulates Tk expression in response to nutrient stress and infection, and is essential for survival of starvation but not infection. These findings suggest that, while the responses to starvation and infection require considerable energy expenditure, distinct signaling pathways participate in generating the metabolic response to each. Thus, the type of energy demand encountered determines the signaling pathway utilized to mobilize lipids.

Results

A GulpR mutant displays decreased numbers of Tk-expressing (Tk+) cells in the AMG and PMG but increased lipid storage in the AMG only

In a previous RNA-seq experiment using Vibrio cholerae-infected whole flies, we noted a positive correlation between the intestinal levels of the short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) acetate during infection and expression of CG32547, a GPCR previously shown to be EEC-specific [–]. We renamed this GPCR GulpR for its action in the setting of nutrient limitation, which we elucidate here. GulpR has two predicted transcripts RC and RD, which encode identical polypeptides. These transcripts differ only in the length of their 3’ untranslated regions. Both consist of 7 exons of which 6 contain coding sequences (S1 Fig) [].

Because acetate prevents lipid accumulation in the Drosophila AMG by increasing Tk expression, we questioned whether GulpR might be involved in regulating Tk expression and/or release []. To test this hypothesis, we first characterized an available GulpR transposon-insertion mutant fly (GulpRf06408) []. This transposon is located at the beginning of intron 3 and, therefore, interrupts both the RC and RD transcripts (S1 Fig). Adult female flies between 4–7 days of age were used to confirm that GulpR transcription was reduced in the intestines of GulpRf06408 flies as compared with control w1118 using primers both upstream of and bridging the transposon insertion (Figs 1A and S1). We then questioned whether GulpR was expressed in Tk+ EECs. To test this, we crossed a Tk> driver shown to principally target Tk+ EECs with two independent GulpRRNAi lines, GulpRJF03036 (RNAi1) and GulpRHMS05678 (RNAi2) [,]. Transcription of GulpR in the intestines of Tk>GulpRRNAi1 and Tk>GulpRRNAi2 flies was significantly decreased compared with Tk> flies (Fig 1B). This confirms that GulpR is present in Tk+ cells. We then quantified Tk+ EECs and lipid accumulation in w1118 and GulpRf06408 flies in the regions of the AMG and PMG shown in Fig 1C. We observed an accumulation of lipids in the AMG of the GulpR mutant but not the PMG. This was accompanied by a reduction in the number of Tk+ EECs in both the AMG and PMG (Fig 1D-1F). To confirm that this was not the result of increased food intake, we performed a feeding assay that showed no difference in intestinal food contents (Fig 1G). We conclude that GulpR regulates Tk expression and/or secretion in both the AMG and PMG, but lipid accumulation only in the AMG.

GulpRRNAi in Tk+ EECs decreases intestinal Tk expression and increases lipid accumulation

To determine whether cell-autonomous GulpR expression is required to maintain Tk levels and lipid homeostasis in the Drosophila intestine, we compared the intestinal phenotype of Tk> flies with Tk>GulpRRNAi1 and Tk>GulpRRNAi2 flies. Like the GulpR mutant, Tk>GulpRRNAi1 and Tk>GulpRRNAi2 flies exhibited an increase in lipid storage in the AMG and a decrease in the number of Tk+ EECs in the AMG and PMG (Fig 2). Because this had not previously been reported, we questioned whether accumulation of lipids in the AMG represented region-specific Tk regulation of lipid homeostasis or a direct action of GulpR []. To explore this, we compared lipid accumulation and Tk staining in the intestines of Tk > TkRNAi flies with that in Tk>GulpRRNAi1, Tk>GulpRRNAi2, and Tk> intestines. In fact, Tk+ EECs were decreased in the intestines of Tk > TkRNAi flies beyond that observed for Tk>GulpRRNAi1 and Tk>GulpRRNAi2 flies but lipid accumulation was observed only in the AMG (Fig 2). These results indicate that GulpR regulates Tk expression in the AMG and PMG, but Tk regulates lipid utilization only in the AMG. We have not yet uncovered a role for Tk in the PMG. We also used an antibody targeting the general EEC marker prospero (pros) to quantify total EEC’s in the AMG and PMG of Tk> and Tk>GulpRRNAi1 flies to evaluate the possibility that decreased Tk+ EECs was the result of an overall decrease in EECs. As shown in S2 Fig, total numbers of pros+ EECs were not significantly different in the AMG and PMG of Tk> and Tk>GulpRRNAi1 flies. A small decrease was noted for Tk > TkRNAi flies. Because EEC Tk expression in Tk > TkRNAi flies is decreased beyond that of Tk>GulpRRNAi1 flies, this suggests that large decreases in Tk expression may impact EEC development. To establish that regulation of Tk expression by GulpR does not represent a developmental phenotype, we used a temperature-sensitive pros driver to conditionally drive activation expression of GulpRRNAi1 and TkRNAi in adulthood. This yielded a similar phenotype similar to that observed for Tk> GulpRRNAi1 and TkRNAi (S3 Fig).

GPCRs may regulate EEP secretion as well as expression. Therefore, we examined the possibility that a block in secretion might result in negative feedback on expression leading to a decrease in Tk+ cells. Bruchpilot (brp) is an exocytosis factor that is essential for neuropeptide release from vesicles at neural synapses [–]. While brp has not been studied in the intestine, it is highly transcribed in EECs but not other intestinal cell types []. Given the similar processes of vesicle release from EECs and neural synapses, we hypothesized that brpRNAi might perform a function in EECs similar to that at neural synapses, and, thus, block Tk release. Tk > brpRNAi resulted in lipid accumulation in the AMG but had no impact on the number of Tk+ EECs (Fig 2). These findings support our hypothesis that brp is essential for Tk release from EECs and, furthermore, suggest that a block in Tk release does not lead to a decrease in Tk expression. Our results establish a role for GulpR in activating Tk expression but do not rule out an additional role for GulpR in Tk secretion.

GulpR activates expression of additional EEPs produced by Tk+ EECs

To further differentiate regulation of EEP transcription and secretion, we conducted an RNA sequencing experiment comparing the intestinal transcriptomes of Tk>GulpRRNA1i and Tk > brpRNAi flies to that of Tk> flies. Using a threshold of 2-fold change and a padj of 0.05, 82 genes were differentially regulated by GulpRRNAi1 with 41 increasing in transcription and 41 decreasing (Fig 3A and S1 Table). Using the same criteria, brpRNAi differentially regulated 124 genes with 78 increased and 46 decreased (Fig 3B and S2 Table). Twenty-nine genes were similarly regulated by the two, suggesting overlapping but distinct functions. Genes whose transcription was uniquely decreased in the intestines of Tk>GulpRRNAi1 flies included Tk as well as two additional EEPs expressed in the same EEC subtype: Neuropeptide F (NPF) and Diuretic hormone 31 (Dh31). In contrast, none of these reached our threshold in Tk > brpRNAi flies. These results were confirmed by qRT-PCR (Fig 3C and 3D).
